title: SLO-preserving pacing shaper with cascading circuit breakers and fidelity multiplexing
creator: Asha Kapoor
description:
Background:
Redwood's hosted API occasionally experiences short-duration demand spikes that push tail latency above SLOs despite autoscaling. Traditional hard-shedding either drops requests (bad UX) or routes to lower-fidelity models blindly, which can violate tenant SLAs and give unpredictable cost behavior. We need a runtime-level mechanism that preserves per-tenant SLOs as much as possible while providing graceful degradation and clear operational signals.

Proposal summary:
Implement a runtime "pacing shaper" that enforces SLO-aware ingress pacing per-tenant and per-route using lightweight leaky-token pacing windows. The shaper integrates with "cascading circuit breakers" (CBs) at three tiers: edge (ingress proxy), regional router, and serving pool. When a CB trips it signals upstream to progressively reduce load via slower pacing windows and selective multiplexing. Introduce "fidelity multiplexing": responses are produced incrementally (thin-first) and enriched only when capacity permits. The runtime will stitch and finalize responses or gracefully yield partial-but-useful outputs.

Goals:
- Keep 95th percentile request latency within SLO for P1 tenants during spikes (target: < SLO + 10% degradation window).
- Minimize hard drops; prefer delayed start / partial responses when feasible.
- Provide deterministic, auditable decisioning so billing and SLAs can be reconciled.

Non-goals:
- This is not a replacement for long-term autoscaling investments. Not addressing multi-model ensemble fallback logic in v1.

High-level design:
1) Pacing shaper: per-tenant token bucket with time-windowed refill tuned by target SLO (derived from tenant SLA and observed p50/p95). Unlike classic admission, pacing softly delays request dispatch to the serving pool. Parameters: window_ms, max_inflight, min_interarrival_ms, soft_drop_threshold.
2) Cascading CBs: three boolean states (Closed, Throttled, Open). Transition logic uses a composite signal: serving-pool queue length, GPU utilization, and recent p95 latency breach count. CB events carry a reason code and suggested pacing multiplier (0.5x, 0.25x, drop).
3) Fidelity multiplexing: API producers implement an incremental output protocol (thin-first kernel). The runtime first generates a lightweight skeleton reply (summaries, top-k candidates, score hints) and streams it immediately. If pacing and capacity allow, a follow-up enrichment step is performed and the final payload is appended or patched. Consumers without streaming support will receive a best-effort finalization or a consistent partial marker.
4) Policy layer: declarative YAML that maps tenants/routes to SLO targets, allowed degradation tiers, and billing reconciliation flags. Operators can set allowed partial-response types per tenant.

Implementation plan (phases):
Phase A (prototype, 2 weeks):
- Runtime: add pacing middleware to ingress proxy (golang) that implements windowed token pacing and emits metrics.
- CB simulator: standalone service that consumes metrics and emits CB state for a test shard.
- Simple multiplexing shim: minimal skeleton payload + finalization path for generation endpoints.
Artifacts: design doc (Confluence) + prototype PR.

Phase B (internal canary, 3 weeks):
- Integrate CB signals into regional router.
- Wire pacing multipliers into serving scheduler (respecting concurrency budgets).
- Add reconciliation pipeline for metering partial vs full responses.
- Add control-plane toggles and tenant policy UI stubs in Console.

Phase C (gradual rollout, 3 weeks):
- Canary 1% tenants (non-critical), monitor p95, error rates, and revenue meter.
- Canary 10% after stability, progressively to 50% with rollback windows.

Acceptance criteria:
- Under a synthetic 5x burst, P1 tenants' p95 remains within configured target in >= 90% of experiments when pacing is enabled and CBs transition as designed.
- Less than 0.5% of requests are hard-dropped during controlled spike tests for canary tenants.
- Billing reconciliation shows partial responses accounted correctly (metering tests).
- Observability: CB transitions and pacing multipliers visible in Console with per-tenant timeline.

Monitoring & alerts:
- New metrics: pacing.window_utilization, pacing.delayed_requests, cb.state_changes, multiplex.enrichment_rate, multiplex.partial_response_fraction.
- Alerts: cb.opens > 3 in 5m for a region (SEV2), pacing.delay_p50 > 300ms for key customers (SEV3).

Security & compliance notes:
- Partial responses must not leak restricted fields; policy layer must include allowlist controls.
- For Private/VPC customers with strict data governance, default behavior is to disable multiplexing unless explicitly permitted.

Testing strategy:
- Unit tests for pacing math, CB transitions, and multiplexing state machine.
- Load tests (k6/pylons) simulating multi-region failover with injected latencies and GPU throttling.
- Chaos test: randomly flip CB states and validate graceful behavior and observability.

Rollout & rollback plan:
- Feature gate at control plane; enable per-tenant.
- Canary plan: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% over 4 weeks with automated regression gates.
- Immediate rollback: disable pacing middleware to return to baseline.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Thin-first vs best-effort finalization: consumers without streaming may see partial markers — product needs to decide default UX.
- Charge model for partial responses: bill for underlying compute used vs unit price for completed token streams. This affects customer UX and accounting complexity.
- Complexity of policy language vs operational safety: simpler policies reduce operator error but limit flexibility.

Links / artifacts:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RR/SLO+Pacing+Shaper+Design
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2418
- Load test dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/ingress/pacing-shaper-load-tests
